SITUATION TENSE.
CANTON'S" OPPOSING FACTIONS.
HOTBED OF INTRIGUE.
Little news has filtered through from Canton but well-informed sources have been reliably informed that the political situation is tense.

Now that there is no common enemy to fight on the field the Kuomintang split has become more open. It seems that the leaders on either side are reluctant to provoke a crisis. Rather, each side is waiting for the other to waver; and hopes exist in Canton political circles that bloodless struggle will ensue.

Fighting does not seem imminent; but troops are being moved about, it is stated, for the purpose of occupying strategic positions and consolidating the rival strengths. There seems little doubt that the so-called Whampoa Cadets (literally translated as Student Soldiers, but really Northern Chinese mercenaries who have experienced several campaigns) under Cheung Kaisek are showing traces of Red influence.

Once again it is the same old competition for sweets of office and power. Difficulty confronts everybody who is not actively engaged in the game, and it is almost impossible to say what armies comprise the opposing factions: However, it is obvious that the leaders with Communistic tendencies are trying to assert a superiority both in the civil and military realms. Intrigue is being combated by intrigue.

It is alleged that unimportant breaches between individual men here and there have led to a breach with General Hsu Shungchi's Cantonese detachments in and around Canton. To complicate the situation further, General Hsu is indirectly accused of invoking the aid of Chan Kwingming's subordinates in preference to turning over territory to "Red soldiers under the Kuomintang.
“BETTER DAILY.”
AN INSTANCE OF " THE WIL TO WIN."
STRIKE POSITION

Whilst there are few outward signs of a general return to work such as will follow when, in His Excellency's words, "the strikers come to their senses," the speech in which he let them fall has created a good impression and led to greater confidence in the determination of the Government to see this thing through," also in the measures they have already taken and those His Excellency indicated were about to be put in hand.

What His Excellency termed the "will to win" was never more strongly in evidence on the part of the general community and a striking instance of the efficient manner in which public services are being maintained is the despatch with which the Home mail arriving by the s.s. Kashgar has been handled at the Post Office. There were 450 bags in all and the sorters, consisting entirely of voluntary workers, got the letters ready for delivery within an hour and a half of the sorting having commenced, i.e., at 10 a.m. to-day. Well might the Superintendent of mails join with Coué in saying "they are getting better and better every day."
SERVANT'S WAGES
KOWLOON CASE TO BE RE-HEARD.

It was stated at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning that the case in which a house coolie was convicted yesterday for leaving his employer's service without notice will be re-opened as, after consideration, it appears to the Magistrate that a certain point in the case is not in accordance with law.

As already reported, Mr. E. W. Hamilton fined the house coolie $25, with the alternative of one month's hard labour, and further forfeited a month's wages in favour of the complainant by ordering the accused to pay $3 representing one week's wages from June 24.

SEAMEN'S ACTION.
RIVER BOATS LEFT TO SKELETON CREW.
WHITE RUSSIANS HELP.

The most important development has been that fores' dowed in yesterday's "Chim Mail," the desertion of whole crows of Chinese semen engaged on the river boats. Two boats arrived from Canton this morning, the Kwong Tung and the Ko Chow, but both are laying-to-at any rate for the present and do not anticipate returning to Canton for some time to come. The Ko Chow's crew deserted in Canton to a man-engineers, quartermasters, firemen and semen (some of them had been in the employment of the owners for eight years). Volunteers were called for among the crew, some of whom were very anxious that the boat should proceed and that they should reach Hongkong acting as firemen. The Captain took the wheel and with the Chief Officer and Engineer doing veoman work the trip was completed without untoward incident in about 11 hours.
The Kwong Tung was not affected to any great extent but she is to leave the wharf and anchor behind Stonecutters later in the day as it is known that the seamen are under orders to leave.

Another boat which is affected, but to what degree it is impossible to sav at the moment, is the Tung On. last seen by the Kwang Tung as she lay at Butterfield and Swire's wharf at Canton. As the Kwongtung passed the Captain of the Tung On held out his hands as if to signify that all the crew had left.

Also in Canton yesterday, believed to be crew-less, was the Charles Hardouin, and the Paul Beau, which was also due to arrive in Hongkong yesterday evening, left Canton at noon with a skeleton crew and has not yet put in. She is doubtless taking no chance and proceeding with caution.

The crew of the Sai On, which was to have left for Canton yesterday, have so far remained loyal and the boat left the wharf as usual. When seen this morning to be no further away than Stonecutters it was at first feared that the seamen had changed their minds at the last moment but it appears that the boat was stopped by the police in order that a search could be carried out in connection with the incident at a compradore's shop on the Praya, reported elsewhere.

The crew of the Macao boat Wing On also deserted to a man when that boat arrived at Macao yesterday, but the skipper was determined to get her back to Hongkong and for that purpose employed a number of White Russians. They did the work efficiently and it would probably be possible to maintain the regular service but it has been decided to lay-to for the present. It is not yet known, how the sister Macao boat to the Wing On, the Chung Cho, has fared regarding crew. She is due back in Hongkong to day.
LAUNCH PIRATES.
CHUNG CHAU SERVICE AFFECTED

Chung Chau residents yesterday had to catch the 5-15 lunch or none at all owing to the pirating of the character of boat which has been taking the place of the regular launch undergoing repair.
This chartered launch, the Po On, in the morning is engaged in another ferry service, namely that to Deep Bay (beyond Castle Peak) and in the course of this it was pirated yesterday, over 20 pirates boarding it and ordering the cox to proceed to Sha Sheung. When the launch arrived there 19 of the passengers were taken ashore, also the boat's accountant. Some articles were also taken from the boat which was released at noon and this morning was to be seen alongside the wharf as usual.

DEFINED.
ISSUES
STRIKERS "NOW COMING TO THEIR SENSES."

That the strike in Hongkong represented an attack against the liberty and existing standards of civilisation as represented here and was not directed against the British Government nor foreigners as such was the main effect of a statement made by His Excellency the Governor, in the Legislative Council yesterday. We had been selected for attack, said His Excellency, because of our propinquity to a district which, owing to a long period of war and mis-Government, was a fertile soil for the cultivation of all the worst growths of Bolshevism, anarchy and Communism.
It was difficult to see in what way any anti-Government or anti-European feeling could be involved in a strike of Chinese barbers, teushops, hairdressers or pork butchers, said His Excellency, Later he congratulated the European community on the confidence they had already given by the manner in which they were carrying on also those sections of the Chinese community who were capable of thinking for themselves and who realised that the issues were as much theirs as ours.

As regarded the present aspect of affairs it was difficult to say anything definite, suf'll His Excellency. There were signs that the strikers were coming to their senses. Many were still going out but many were returning to work and he was not without hope that common sense

would prevail over ignorance and fear. Meanwhile the community had to carry on and see this thing through. The prospects were not such as to cause any alarm. The food supplies in so far as the Europeans were concerned, were simple and could be easily replenished. The same probably, was the case with regard to the Chinese community and here there was the additional advantage—that should there be any prospect of supplies running short the consumption could be diminished by deporting unproductive consumers.

We were, of course, experiencing loss of trade, considerable, inconvenience and minor hardships but His Excellency was confident both as to the power and the will of the community to endure them as long as was necessary. The inconveniences were not entirely on one side, however, and he trusted that the strikers would shortly find that the game was not worth the candle. Drastic measures had, find to be taken and they would if necessary be made more drastic. He (His Excellency) was as fold as any man of getting his own way. He had always preferred to do so by convincing others that his way was the right way. But argument required two sides and if the other side had no reasons to advance to support their point of view it became necessary to take other measures.
“Idle Mouths.”

"We find now," said His Excellency, "that people will not work. They advance no reasons and we cannot discuss the matter. All we can say is if you do not want to, don't but we cannot number this small area with idle mouths, and if you will not work you must leave us! We stated on a small scale and invited some of those whose presence could most easily be dispensed with to seek other spheres of activity, to the number of 100. If necessary that process will be continued and intensified. If necessary I should have no hesitation in deporting from the Colony every adult who did not show by working that he was a useful member of the Community. As the poor said revolutions are not made with rosewater neither are they suppressed by it and this strike amounts to a revolution against law and order."

PRAYA STIR.
COMPRADORE'S SHOP EXPLOSION.

Much commotion was caused yesterday evening by an explosion in a compradore and stevedore's shop on the Praya, not far from the Central Fire Station. A passer-by is said to have thrown a detonator in and then made good his escape.
No one was arrested at the time but as the result of raids on suspected places several suspects were taken to the police station. They were found not to have been concerned in the matter.
No one was injured as a result of the explosion which considerably damaged the front of the shop. This morning armed guards and Chinese special constables were on guard outside the premises.

pretence had been dropped that the so-called strike was in sympathy with those who had suffered as a result of incidents in Shanghai and other ports and it must now be clear even to the most confused behind that it was not concerned with happenings elsewhere. Nothing the Hongkong Government could do or refrain from doing could have the slightest effect on the negotiations taking place between the authorities of Shanghai and the Governments of Peking or any other parties whatever; nor could any negotiations have any influence upon our affairs. In this matter Hongkong stood alone.
Workers' Folly.

It would appear from what had taken place during the last fortnight, said His Excellency, that the main reason for the spread of the strike wa the cowardice and folly of the working classes who allowed themselves to be intimidated by the merest shadow of threats. It was difficult to deal with the situation when through gross cowardice, labourers, in spite of offers of handsome rewards, would not hand over to the police those who threaten them with violence for doing what every man had a right to—continue his lawful vocation. "I have almost completed arrangements, the details of which I must withhold, else their efficiency should suffer," said His Excellency, "which will enable us to be fairly certain of catching such intimidators and under a regulation issued to day they will be dealt with in a manner likely to appeal to their deepest feelings—i.e., by the cat."

Thanks to the activities of the police and members of the public—European and Chinese—to whom he tendered thanks, it had been possible to catch some dozen of these scoundrels, although owing to delay in the issue of the regulation these would escape this provision. It was not intended, however, that they should purge their offences in jail where accommodation and food was superior to that being received by those strikers seeking the hospitality of Canton. They would be given the opportunity of proving their value to the community by undertaking useful—though somewhat unattractive—duties in connection with the sanitation of the Colony.

His Excellency asked the public to realise that it did not follow that the Government was doing nothing because it did not talk about it and said that there were occasions when it was wiser to say nothing in order that measures about to be taken might be the more successful. He asked the public to help by not believing rumours until the Government had confirmed them and not to pass them on whether or not they believed them in the first place. His Excellency referred to the rumours which had been spread of men, being stabbed for staying at their work and quoted two cases where they had originated from bodies of people who had died from natural causes being placed in the street. The police, he said, picked up on an average something like eight bodies a day in this manner.
The public could also help by attempting to instil into servants remaining loyal that the best way of dealing with an intimidator was to intimidate him. If the intimidator injured him the "cat" could redress the balance, whereas if his injured the intimidator it was not only the intimidator's fault, but the loyal servant if he handed the man over to the police would receive a handsome reward.
If these measures were adopted His Excellency was confident that intimidation would quickly cease and business could be gone about in peace.
TYPHOON WARNINGS.
MESSAGES RECEIVED FROM PRATAS.
"QUITE SATISFACTORY."

The welcome news that wireless communication with Pratas Shoal had already been established and that a regular service was expected to be instituted before the end of the present typhoon season was made in the course of discussion at the meeting of the Finance Committee meeting which followed yesterday's Legislative Council meeting.

The great help as regards typhoon warnings of regular messages from a point where the future course of the typhoon is so often determined has been emphasised from time to time and when the negotiations broke down for the building of a meteorological station under the negis of the Hongkong Government the Chinese Maritime Customs, under the Chinese Admiralty, guaranteed that they themselves would provide such a station. After considerable delay the work was put in hand and the work was promised to be completed by October of this year.
The matter arose yesterday out
The matter arose yesterday out of a vote of $2,000 on account of the Royal Observatory, other charges, meteorological telegrams.

The Chairman (the Colonial Secretary) said:—These meteorological telegrams were paid out of the Colonial Secretariat vote for some time, but the number of stations with which we are in communication has increased and the cost has increased a great deal. It is proposed to take a separate vote to cover the cost instead of supplementing our office vote here.
Hon. Mr. Holyoak: In connection with the vote do I understand that _communication_ has been established with Pratas. Shoal already?

The Chairman: We have had messages from Pratas Shoal, but unfortunately: Cape D'Aguilar was only working 600 metres and Pratas Shoal 750, so that we are arranging now for certain times when we shall be ready to receive their messages at the 750 length.
Hon. Mr. Holyoak: Is it in actual operation?
The Chairman: It is quite satisfactory. I should not be surprised if it is sufficiently advanced to receive communications before the end of the typhoon season.
LOCAL SHARES.
FURTHER EXTENSION OF PERIOD OF SETTLEMENT.

When the Bill relating to the postponement of the June Settlement came before the Legislative Council yesterday, the Attorney-General, Sir Henry Pollock, K.C., explained that it had been found convenient to make the postponement of Settlement Day extend over a period of four days, that was to say, from July 14 to July 17 inclusive so as to allow full time for the carrying out of the settlement and any matters of adjustment and accommodation which might seem desirable in connection with it.
The rate of interest (8 per cent.) which was to be charged was considered a reasonable rate, said the Attorney-General; it was approximately the mortgage rate now ruling in the Colony.

The intention of the Government to push the Bill through in one reading was not proceeded with the first reading only being made. The remaining stages would be put through at a special meeting of the Council to be held to-morrow (Saturday) at noon.
STOLEN FIREWOOD
FURTHER OFFENDERS PROSECUTED.

Another batch of illicit firewood hunters were brought before Mr. S. B. B. McElderry at the Central Magistracy this morning. They were arrested by Sergeant McDonald at Kennedy Road with a large quantity of cut pine wood.
His Worship imposed fines of $10, or two weeks' hard labour, on four men, and sentenced a boy to six strokes of the birch. An old woman, who was also one of the offenders, was discharged with a caution as it was stated that she assisted the police officers by giving information leading to the arrest of two of the men after they escaped.
